title: How Black Friday Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Black Friday, the American shopping day after Thanksgiving. They cover the term's origins (late-19th/early-20th century Thanksgiving parades with Santa, and the 1960s Philadelphia police and bus driver usage tied to the Army-Navy game crowds, versus the mistaken "in the black" theory), how retailers promoted it as the start of holiday shopping (including the 2004 switch to calling it the busiest day), the spinoff promotions Cyber Monday and Small Business Saturday, retailers pushing into Thanksgiving itself, the economics of doorbuster bait-and-switch deals, violent and deadly incidents (the 2008 Valley Stream Walmart stampede that killed employee Jdimytai Damour, the 2008 Palm Desert Toys R Us shooting, the 2011 Los Angeles pepper spraying), worker concerns, and counter-movements like Buy Nothing Day and Singles Day in China.

segments.title: Opening banter and Black Friday skepticism
segments.summary: Hosts banter about Jerry's presence and whether they have ever attended a Black Friday sale, and joke about the divisive nature of the shopping day.

segments.title: What Black Friday is and its early origins
segments.summary: Black Friday is defined as the busiest US shopping day, the day after Thanksgiving. Its roots trace to late-19th and early-20th century department store promotions tied to Thanksgiving parades featuring Santa Claus.

segments.title: Origin of the name Black Friday
segments.summary: The term is traced to 1960s Philadelphia, where police, cab and bus drivers and city workers used it for the chaotic day when out-of-town crowds came for the Army-Navy game. Retailers later sought a friendlier origin story. The 'in the black' profit explanation is described as a myth.

segments.title: Holiday retail spending and Black Friday as a sales kickoff
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how much is spent during the November and December holiday season, a National Retail Federation forecast, and how the busiest-shopping-day label was promoted starting around 2004 to spread shopping out over weeks.

segments.title: Cyber Monday, Small Business Saturday, and retail marketing myths
segments.summary: Retailers created Cyber Monday in 2005 and American Express created Small Business Saturday in 2010, extending the promotional period. The hosts note these were self-fulfilling marketing ideas.

segments.title: Thanksgiving store openings and shortened shopping season
segments.summary: Stores began opening on Thanksgiving, starting with Walmart in 2012, and in 2013 more chains including Macy's, Kmart and Sears opened on the holiday. The hosts discuss how Thanksgiving 2013 falling late shortens the season and how other countries lack a Black Friday.

segments.title: Doorbusters and bait-and-switch deals
segments.summary: Doorbusters are limited deep discounts on a few items, which the hosts describe as bait and switch that draws shoppers in to buy regular-priced goods.

segments.title: 2008 Valley Stream Walmart stampede
segments.summary: A crowd of roughly two thousand gathered at a Valley Stream, Long Island Walmart on Thanksgiving 2008. The barricade was breached, and the crowd crushed people against the doors. Employee Jdimytai Damour was trampled and died. A pregnant woman, Lean Lockley, was pulled inside by workers.

segments.title: Other Black Friday violence and crowd safety
segments.summary: The hosts cover the 2008 Palm Desert Toys R Us shooting between two husbands, the 2011 Los Angeles Walmart pepper-spray incident involving a mother defending her children, and general trampling videos. They note that planners can be the most aggressive shoppers.

segments.title: Buy Nothing Day, Singles Day, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Buy Nothing Day, started by Ted Dave and promoted by Adbusters, and China's Singles Day on November 11, which Alibaba promoted. They close with Thanksgiving wishes and website information.
